text:
Interviewer: This is a United States Holocaust Memorial Museum interview with Peter Miller, on September 16th, 2010, in Silver Spring, Maryland, in Mr. Miller’s home, and thank you very much for agreeing to see us, to be re-interviewed by —
Interviewee: You’re welcome.
Interviewer: — the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. And I will start with trying to lay the groundwork, trying to find out the world — a little bit about the world you were born into. Can you tell me where you were born, when, your name, your parents’ names, and we’ll go from there.
Interviewee: Okay, I was born in Regensburg, Germany, which is up the Danube from Straubing, where my family lived, probably because they had better medical care there than in Straubing, so it happened there. My name f — w — at that time was Frankeir Miller, but when I came to United States and I got my citizenship paper, I did not like the Germanic name of Frankeir, so I had it legally changed to Frank, and I took the middle name of David, which is in honor of my grandfather.
Interviewer: I see. What year were you born? What’s the date of your birth?
Interviewee: May 19, 1930.
Interviewer: Do you have brothers and sisters?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: You were an only child.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Was yours a large family?
Interviewee: On my father’s side, my father had four brothers and four sisters, and some of them weren’t living any more when I was born, and I was the youngest of about oh, seven, eight grandchildren. That’s on my father’s side. On my mother’s side, my mother had a sister and a brother. Brother who had a PhD. in chemistry from the University of Heidelberg, but due to the situation in Germany, he couldn’t get a job there. So he emigrated to Holland, and he worked for Organon, which is the big pharmaceutical company there. And he was part of the earl — original research for the conjugated estrogens.
Interviewer: I see. Could you spell the name of that research company so that we can —
Interviewee: Organon, o-r-g-a-n-o-n.
Interviewer: Organon, okay.
Interviewee: And they’re in — located in a place called Oss, o-s-s, in Holland.
Interviewer: What was — what was your father’s profession, or what — how did he make a living?
Interviewee: My father was a cattle and horse dealer. He would buy cattle from farmers, resell it to other farmers. He’d buy cattle to be slaughtered. As far as the horses went, he would go every year at the German-Belgium border, where they had a type of horse like the Clydesdale, heavy work horses. He would buy them as colts, transport them to Bavaria and then resell them to farmers, who raised them.
Interviewer: Tell — can you tell me — th-this is just pure coincidence. This morning we had an interview with somebody whose father was also in the cattle market business. Was this a fai — was this an area of activity that there were more Jews than in other areas, or was this just a pure coincidence that we were —
Interviewee: I think was — that I — I don’t know for a fact, but I think a lot of Jews, for instance, our family, my father and his father were — worked together. An uncle by the name of Barry Miller also was in the cattle and horse business in Regensburg, which is a little way up the da — Danube. There were more Millers in the cattle and horse business, and they more or less worked together. And I was told that they had the largest cattle business in Bavaria.
Interviewer: I see. Okay, okay, so that — it gives us a little bit of sense of the wider context.
Interviewee: I don’t know how true it is about the size of it, but that’s what I heard.
Interviewer: Okay. And your mother, was she involved in her — your dad’s business as well, or wa —
Interviewee: Well no, she was just a regular housewife.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: And the funny thing is, her father was in the horse business.
Interviewer: What was her name?
Interviewee: Her name — her name is Iris Bergs.
Interviewer: How do — i-r-i-s is her first —
Interviewee: I-r-i-s, and last name B-e-r-g-s.
Interviewer: B-e-r-g-s. And your father’s first name was?
Interviewee: Smert. S-m-e-r-t.
Interviewer: Smert Miller, okay. Would you say that your family was a well-to-do family?
Interviewee: Well, as a child I wouldn’t know that much about finance then, but we were pretty well off, I would think.
Interviewer: Did you have nannies, did you have servants at home?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Did you have housekeepers and things like that?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Yeah. What are some of your earliest memories from your childhood?
Interviewee: Well, my mother was from a village in Buttenwiessen which was also in Bavaria, which was a good distance away, and we used to go to Buttenwiessen frequently.
Interviewer: Buttenwiessen?
Interviewee: Yes. It’s b-u-t-t-e-n-w-i-e-s-s-e-n.
Interviewer: Was it a fun thing for a child to do when you went to Buttenwiessen?
Interviewee: Well, I never got there after I was four years old because my grandfather died and Grandma came to live with us.
Interviewer: Ah, I see. So it was — it was something that happened only in those first four years of your life?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: And what memories do you have of Buttenwiessen?
Interviewee: My cousin and I, who — who was — he was a year and a half older, we went with my grandfather to — one time while he was out selling a horse or something, and there was a very steep place there, which is made out of concrete and we use it like a slide and we slid down. I — they did something that they considered impossible, I got home in leather pants.
Interviewer: So you — did you wear lederhosen?
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: That is a very — I mean, that’s quite an achievement, cause those are tough pieces of leather there. Any other memories from that time, of your grandfather —
Interviewee: Well, I re — I remember the first Seders I went to.
Interviewer: Mm-hm, what were they like?
Interviewee: They were just a lot of fun.
Interviewer: Well, tell somebody who’s not Jewish a little bit about Seders in Germany at that time, cause I wouldn’t know.
Interviewee: Well — well, the family came together and there was a lot of singing, lot of good food, and we went through the whole Haggadah.
Interviewer: A-And that is a prayer?
Interviewee: The Haggadah is the prayer book that they use for the Seder.
Interviewer: I see. Okay, thank you. And is thi — was this something that was very traditional? Was your family a very religious family?
Interviewee: Yeah, we were brought up Orthodox.
Interviewer: I see. Okay. And wa — was that something that almost all Jews in smaller cities and towns would — would observe?
Interviewee: Well, I don’t know about — cause I was just a little one, so —
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: — I don’t know. In Straubing we had one synagogue an it was Orthodox and Buttenwiessen was one synagogue and that was Orthodox. In fact, Buttenwiessen at the turn of the century, that’s back in 1900, was about 70 percent Jewish.
Interviewer: Did you have any contact with Gentile Germans at all? Do you remember, from ger —
Interviewee: Oh yeah, when — when I was in school, in the first grade, I was entered into the — well, it was called the Protestant school. I was entered there and there were just two of us in the class, two Jewish children. The other one was a girl who — who I happen to know cause we grew up together, we were the same age. And I had the lovely experience of being expelled from school in the first grade because I hit a Nazi child and I was too dangerous to be left with them.
Interviewer: Oh dear, and you were how old?
Interviewee: Six.
Interviewer: And di-did you know the full reasons why this was happening?
Interviewee: Well, yeah, th-the wa — w-we — we knew that, being Jewish that we were just being hit upon and it just so happened this child was about three years older than me and a foot taller, and he started picking on me. So my dad being in the cattle and horse business, I ran into the house, got a horsewhip and hit him once with it. And there is a picture of me with the horsewhip way up on top.
Interviewer: Oh, we will take a look at that photograph later. And — and that was enough to make that happen.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: And that was —
Interviewee: And I was out of school, my par — parents protested and what does a kid know, and after six weeks, after a lot of red tape going through the — with the — with the German government, the — I finally was allowed to go back to school. And at the end of the year, all the Jewish kids were expelled from the school.
Interviewer: So this would have been 1935 - ’36?
Interviewee: Thirty si — 30 s — either ’36 or ’37. I started school in ’36, so I don’t know what was —
Interviewer: Yeah, probably —
Interviewee: — after new year, probably ’37.
Interviewer: Was that — is that your most vivid memory of coming — you know, sort of like head on into Nazism and you know, when you experience it, or did you have other things that —
Interviewee: Well, you could walk down the street — I mean, my parents ar — I w — I was — they let me go on the streets by myself and I’d see German storm troopers, SS men, SA men walking on the streets, and I — I was just a kid, so they didn’t know who I was, so I just walked everywhere, I
